source_text: καὶ δὴ τῆς κατὰ τὸν γνωστικὸν ἡμῖν ὡς εἰπεῖν ἀπαθείας, καθ᾿ ἣν ἡ τελείωσις τοῦ πιστοῦ δι᾿ ἀγάπης »εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον. εἰς μέτρον ἡλικίας« προβαίνουσα ἀφικνεῖται, ἐξομοιουμένη θεῷ, »ἰσάγγελος« ἀληθῶς γενομένη. πολλὰ μὲν καὶ ἄλλα ἐκ γραφῆς μαρτύρια ἔπεισι παρατίθεσθαι. ἄμεινον δὲ οἶμαι ὑπερθέσθαι τὴν τοιαύτην φιλοτιμίαν διὰ τὸ μῆκος τοῦ λόγου, τοῖς πονεῖν ἐθέλουσι καὶ προσεκπονεῖν τὰ δόγματα κατ᾿ ἐκλογὴν τῶν γραφῶν ἐπιτρέψαντα. μιᾶς δ᾿ οὖν διὰ βραχυτάτων ἐπιμνησθήσομαι, ὡς μὴ ἀνεπισημείωτον παραλιπεῖν τὸν τόπον. λέγει γὰρ ἐν τῇ προτέρᾳ [τῆς] πρὸς Κορινθίους ἐπιστολῇ ὁ θεῖος ἀπόστολος· »τολμᾷ τις ὑμῶν πρᾶγμα ἔχων πρὸς τὸν ἕτερον κρίνεσθαι ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδίκων καὶ οὐχὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων; ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ἅγιοι τὸν κόσμον κρινοῦσι;« καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. μεγίστης δ᾿ οὔσης τῆς περικοπῆς. ταῖς ἐπικαίροις τῶν ἀποστολικῶν συγχρώμενοι λέξεσι, διὰ βραχυτάτων ἐξ ἐπιδρομῆς οἷον μεταφράζοντες τὴν ῥῆσιν, τὴν διάνοιαν τοῦ ῥητοῦ τοῦ ἀποστόλου παραστήσομεν. καθ᾿ ἣν τοῦ γνωστικοῦ τὴν τελειότητα ὑπογράφει. οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀδικεῖσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ ἀδικεῖν ἵστησι τὸν γνωστικὸν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀμνησίκακον εἶναι διδάσκει, μηδὲ εὔχεσθαι κατὰ τοῦ ἀδικήσαντος ἐπιτρέπων· οἶδεν γὰρ καὶ τὸν κύριον ἄντικρυς »εὔχεσθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐχθρῶν« παραγγείλαντα. τὸ μὲν οὖν »ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδίκων κρίνεσθαι« τὸν ἠδικημένον φάσκει οὐδὲν ἀλλ᾿ ἢ ἀνταποδοῦναι βούλεσθαι δοκεῖν καὶ ἀνταδικῆσαι δεύτερον ἐθέλειν, ὅπερ ὁμοίως ἐστὶν ἀδικῆσαι καὶ αὐτόν. τὸ δὲ »ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων κρίνεσθαι« ἐθέλειν τινὰς λέγειν ἐμφαίνει τοὺς δι᾿ εὐχῆς τοῖς ἀδικήσασιν ἀνταποδοθῆναι τὴν πλεονεξίαν αἰτουμένους, καὶ εἶναι μὲν τῶν προτέρων τοὺς δευτέρους ἀμείνους, οὐδέπω δὲ ἀπαθεῖς, ἢν μὴ ἀμνησίκακοι τέλεον γενόμενοι κατὰ τὴν τοῦ κυρίου διδασκαλίαν προσεύξωνται καὶ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐχθρῶν. Καλὸν οὖν καὶ φρένας καλὰς ἐκ μετανοίας αὐτοὺς τῆς εἰς τὴν πίστιν μεταλαβεῖν. εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἐχθροὺς ἡ ἀλήθεια τοὺς παραζηλοῦντας κεκτῆσθαι δοκεῖ, ἀλλ᾿ οὔ τί γε αὐτὴ διεχθρεύεταί τινι. »ὅ« τε γὰρ »θεὸς ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους τὸν αὑτοῦ ἐπιλάμπει ἥλιον« καὶ τὸν κύριόν γε αὐτὸν ἐπὶ δικαίους ἔπεμψεν καὶ ἀδίκους, ὅ τε ἐξομοιοῦσθαι βιαζόμενος θεῷ, διὰ τῆς πολλῆς ἀμνησικακίας »ἀφεὶς ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά« (οἶον κατὰ πάντα τὸν βίον καὶ καθ᾿ ὅλην τὴν κοσμικὴν περιήλυσιν ἑβδομάσιν ἀριθμουμέναις σημαινομένην), παντί τῳ χρηστεύεται, εἰ καί τις τὸν πάντα τοῦτον ἐν σαρκὶ βιοὺς χρόνον ἀδικεῖ τὸν γνωστικόν. οὐ γὰρ τὴν κρίσιν μόνην ἄλλοις ἐπιτρέπειν ἀξιοῖ τὸν σπουδαῖον τῶν ἠδικηκότων αὐτόν, ἀλλὰ καὶ παρ᾿ ἐκείνων αἰτεῖσθαι τῶν κριτῶν βούλεται τὸν δίκαιον τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τοῖς εἰς αὐτὸν πεπλημμεληκόσι, καὶ εἰκότως· εἴ γε τὸ ἐκτὸς μόνον καὶ τὸ περὶ σῶμα, κἂν μέχρι θανάτου προβαίνῃ.
pass_a_gloss: And so, concerning the apatheia that is, so to speak, ours according to the gnostic, by which the perfection of the faithful advances through love 'to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature', and reaches, being assimilated to God, truly having become 'equal to angels'. Many other testimonies from scripture are about to be presented. But I think it is better to surpass such ambition because of the length of the discourse, having permitted those who wish to labor and toil over the dogmas by selection of the scriptures. So then, I will remind you of one thing in brief, so as not to leave the passage unremarked. For the divine apostle says in the first epistle to the Corinthians: 'Does any of you dare, having a matter against another, to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world?' And the things that follow. Since the passage is very large, by synchronizing with the opportune words of the apostolic writings, as if translating the phrase in brief, we will present the thought of the apostle who has written it, according to which he describes the perfection of the gnostic. For he does not establish the gnostic only on being wronged rather than wronging, but also teaches to be forgetful of evils, not permitting to pray against the one who has wronged. For he knows that the Lord has commanded 'to pray for enemies'. So then, the phrase 'to be judged before the unrighteous' says that the one who has been wronged wishes to do nothing else than to repay and to retaliate, which is equally to do wrong and to wrong himself. But the phrase 'to be judged before the saints' says that some wish to say that those who have wronged them should repay the excess, and that they are better than the former ones, but not yet apathetic, unless they become completely forgetful of evils, having prayed according to the Lord's teaching and for their enemies. It is good, therefore, for them to have good minds from repentance, having partaken of faith. For if truth seems to acquire enemies who are jealous, yet it does not hate anyone. For 'God causes his sun to shine on the righteous and the unrighteous' and he sent the Lord upon the righteous and the unrighteous. The one who is forcing himself to be assimilated to God, through much forgetfulness of evils, 'forgiving seventy times seven' (as it were, throughout the whole life and throughout the whole cosmic cycle, indicated by the number seventy), shows kindness to everyone, even if someone wrongs the gnostic all the time he lives in the flesh. For he does not think it worthy to permit judgment to others only, but also to ask from those who judge for the forgiveness of sins to those who have sinned against him, and rightly so. For if what is outside only and what is about the body, even if it proceeds to death.
pass_b_english: And so the *apatheia* that belongs to us, as it were, by way of the gnostic advances through love "to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature" and reaches its goal, becoming assimilated to God and truly "equal to angels" (Eph 4:13). Many other scriptural testimonies could be brought forward, but I think it better to forgo that ambition because of the length of the discourse, leaving those who wish to labor and toil over the doctrines by a selection from the Scriptures to do so. I will, however, recall one passage in brief so as not to leave the place unremarked. For the divine apostle says in the first epistle to the Corinthians, "Does any of you dare, having a matter against another, to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world?" and what follows (1 Cor 6:1). Since the passage is very large, we will present the apostle's thought by synchronizing with the opportune words of the apostolic writings, as it were translating the phrase in brief, according to which he describes the perfection of the gnostic. For he does not establish the gnostic only on the ground of being wronged rather than wronging, but also teaches him to be forgetful of evils, not permitting him to pray against the one who wronged him. For he knows that the Lord commanded "to pray for enemies" (Matt 5:44). So then, the phrase "to be judged before the unrighteous" means that the wronged person wishes nothing other than to repay and to retaliate, which is equally to do wrong himself. But the phrase "to be judged before the saints" indicates that some wish to have the excess returned to those who wronged them by prayer, and these are better than the former ones, yet not yet *apathetic*, unless they become completely forgetful of evils, having prayed according to the Lord's teaching and for their enemies. It is good, therefore, for them to acquire sound minds from repentance, having partaken of faith. For even if the truth seems to acquire enemies who are jealous, it does not hate anyone. For "God causes his sun to shine on the righteous and the unrighteous" (Matt 5:45), and he sent the Lord upon the righteous and the unrighteous. The one who forces himself to be assimilated to God, through much forgetfulness of evils, "forgiving seventy times seven" (Matt 18:22) — that is, throughout the whole life and throughout the whole cosmic cycle, signified by the number seventy — shows kindness to everyone, even if someone wrongs the gnostic all the time he lives in the flesh. For he does not think it worthy to entrust judgment to others only, but also to ask from those who judge for the forgiveness of sins against him, and rightly so; for if the injury is only what is outside and concerns the body, even if it proceeds to death.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a more fluent version with necessary scripture citations (Eph 4:13, 1 Cor 6:1, Matt 5:44, Matt 5:45, Matt 18:22) which are required for clarity in patristic studies. The translation of 'ἀμνησίκακον' as 'forgetful of evils' is consistent. The parenthetical explanation of 'seventy times seven' is correctly handled.
